"Increasingly, companies are starting to realize that they need their employees to be patriotic.

Today, tech is actually the locus of international great power competition. 

China's attempt to build a technosphere that can dominate the American technosphere is critical to your business, but also to the American state, to power and independence. 

So much to the surprise of both the tech world and the political world, they've been driven in on each other, and there's a kind of re-nationalization of tech.

If you're a legacy multinational, free trade is the essence of your business. I need financial markets, labor markets, and manufactured good markets that are seamless and open. 

But if you're a tech company, you don't. Google is not importing and exporting a lot of goods. 

You're much more concerned about security of supply chain, security of intellectual property."

Walter Russell Mead (@wrmead) shares a fascinating dispatch on how fast the war in Ukraine is changing, and what it means for the US military:

"The first time I went to Ukraine after the war, I went to this drone factory, and it really was remarkable because in real time they were starting to get results from the battlefield, and then they were adapting.

But at that time it was very simplistic stuff. They were getting kids' toy trucks and re-engineering them into drones, ground drones that could put a landmine on a tank.

I was back there a couple of months ago, and the advances are just unbelievable. The intensity is the same, but the scope of change is amazing.

I talked to people who said that they don't treat bullet wounds anymore because it's all drones.

The Ukraine war is no longer a battalion over here shooting at a battalion over there.

With these drones, you have this gray zone, where at most you'd have a couple of soldiers together.

One of the hardest problems in warfare now is, how do you evacuate someone who's wounded?

They're having to build a new kind of ground drone that can go retrieve a person, cover them with a metal shield, and wheel them out.

Even to do this, you need a whole team of drones working with this thing because they're looking for other drones that would try to attack this.

They tell me they had one soldier that it took 63 days to get evacuated after a wound.

This is so unlike what war was even six years ago.

If the tank and the rifle are becoming as obsolete as the cavalry charge and the sword, what kind of forces do you need?

We're actually the most vulnerable to technological change, because we've got so many tanks.

If the tank becomes useless, that's more of a problem for us than it is for somebody who's figured out the tank killer."

MetaDAO is rethinking capital formation for startups.

Most launchpads help projects raise money and then step away. MetaDAO uses token markets to govern some of the capital decisions that come next.

Capital raised through the platform enters a DAO treasury with spending limits. When a project seeks more funding or wants to change how its treasury is used, it can submit a proposal to a decision market. Traders estimate what the token would be worth if the proposal passes or fails, and the difference between those prices determines the outcome.

Four approved proposals have raised another $13.34M for MetaDAO itself since launch. Two passed only after earlier versions failed and the terms changed. The same process has returned remaining capital to investors when projects were wound down.

This model depends on active tokenholders. One restructuring passed with only seven wallets and less than $700 in volume. Across 12 launches, a median 52% of allocated wallets sold some tokens within seven days. It remains unclear whether launch recipients will become long-term owners.

The opportunity is larger than a better token launchpad. If tokenization becomes a meaningful way to fund operating businesses, MetaDAO could develop into a founder platform for a new generation of companies raising capital online.

From the Bitcoin pivot through June 2026, common shares increased by roughly 1.13bn. 60%+ of those came after June 2025 after the stock peaked. 

In fairness to management, as far as I can tell the Series 10 ratchet was disclosed in the March 2024 annual report just days before the Bitcoin pivot, and again in the March 2025 annual report. (Happy to be corrected here).

We should also concede the history: Simon was running a tiny distressed microcap when Series 10 was designed in...2022? A huge equity incentive in that situation is not that crazy.

So this was not hidden. An investor doing the work could have found it. The trickiness of dealing with Japanese disclosures, despite my fluency in Japanese, thankfully kept me from owning 3350 in any size after we exited that month.

Management also did a good job growing BTC per share. Had they simply tied comp to that, they still could have made $$$ for the accretion. They did their jobs.

Unfortunately, the windfall produced by the 20% ratchet has become grotesque relative to the company’s current market cap and the stock’s performance since the peak, and leaves management imperfectly aligned with shareholders from here.

Disclosure: I bought a little today. The stock is cheap, I'm more bullish on Bitcoin these days and more willing to take varying exposures. It's not so hard, though perhaps personally a bit expensive, to make things right going forward.

Chamath Warns: Your AI Data Isn’t as Private as You Think

Today's statement from @OpenAI on the Navier-Stokes Problem and whether it used recent user data to boost its own capabilities:

“While unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.”

Here's what @chamath had to say on AI's fragile privacy and the ZDR myth back in July:

“Privacy in AI is very fragile and it's very brittle. There are all kinds of non-obvious data leak vectors lurking in AI.

If you think that you're going to flip a ZDR switch, zero data retention, which is the magic term that the industry uses to tell you that everything's going to be okay.

I think the answer and the message should be, ‘It's not going to be okay because you can't guarantee any of it.’

So the model companies, when they give you these zero data retention policies, are probably trying their best.

But I think the reality is you are leaking information where you don't know it. And they, despite their best efforts, may still have trapdoors that they don't even know about until it's figured out by somebody else.

You need an independent third-party layer to interface to these models to manage this exposure, because there are trapdoors everywhere.”

i've been grinding hard for over a year now. if you are over 35 years old and have 30+ pounds to lose, here's my advice:

- the first step is understanding that something in your lifestyle is very broken. probably not just one thing, either
- you didn't gain all of that weight in a few months, nor will you lose it in a few months. to make it truly sustainable and fueled by permanent lifestyle changes, adjust your time horizon to 1-2 years
- focus on improving your fitness first rather than losing weight, with a foundation of progressive overload resistance training (lifting  heavy weights to within ~3 reps of failure) at least 2x per week some other activity you enjoy 2x per week (for me it's yoga). make sure you walk long distances on off days, and on every other day that you reasonably can
- spend ~3-4 months building up muscle (especially if you are de-conditioned) before making big changes to your diet
- cook your own meals for 80% to 90% of what you eat. meal prep absolutely works if you don't eat junk snacks in-between meals (look for recipes on YouTube). use AI to create healthy, batch recipes of your favorite foods if needed. cook batches of 6-8 servings and freeze them in high quality containers designed for this purpose. plan out what you will eat in advance the next day
- prioritize protein intake (up to 1 gram per pound of target bodyweight, though i personally do closer to 0.75-0.8 g). don't regularly eat junk carbs (like chips, candy, and cakes). eat only when you are hungry, but try to get 3 meals per day to keep your protein intake consistent
- when you start to lose fat, your appearance might not change much due to muscle backfilling it. you may go ~6 months without noticing any big visual changes. monitor body fat mass vs lean muscle mass using either dexa scan or a well-calibrated impedance sensor scale for directional data
- so instead, focus on your improved fitness, feeling in your body, and how your clothes start to fit. forget the number on the scale. it will drop when it is time
- losing fat is like removing sheets of paper from a roll of paper towels. when there are 100 sheets on there, if you remove one, you can barely see it. when you are down to 10-20 sheets, removing one sheet is noticeable

if you put in the work consistently, and are patient and focus on the right goals (improving your health, and weight loss is just one part of it) then you can achieve your goals

get out there and crush it 💪

After reading this, I can’t shake the feeling that we may already be living in a Three-Body world—one in which humanity is gradually, and perhaps inevitably, dividing itself into three camps: the Adventists, the Redemptionists, and the Survivors.

The Adventists want the Trisolarans to come. They see the arrival of a superior intelligence not as an existential threat, but as a potential replacement for a civilization they believe has reached its limits.

The Redemptionists also believe the Trisolarans can save us—but they hope that the two civilizations can coexist, with superior intelligence serving as a means of transcending the flaws of human civilization rather than replacing it.

The Survivors, by contrast, ask a much more primitive question: How do we survive the Trisolarans? For them, the preservation of human agency and human civilization takes precedence over the promise of whatever the future intelligence might bring.

What makes the analogy increasingly unsettling is the rapid emergence of superintelligence.

Perhaps we have already begun to fall, consciously or unconsciously, into these three camps. Some are eagerly anticipating the arrival of something greater than ourselves. Some believe AI will ultimately redeem humanity from many of the constraints that have defined our civilization. And some are increasingly preoccupied with a more fundamental question: whether humans will remain the ones making the decisions in the world we are creating.

The most interesting question, then, may not be whether superintelligence will transform human civilization. That increasingly seems inevitable.

The deeper question is which of these three visions of the future will ultimately prevail—and what happens when the people holding them begin competing for control over the intelligence that will shape that future?

Perhaps the future of AI will be determined not simply by how intelligent machines become, but by the relative dynamics and power of the Adventists, the Redemptionists, and the Survivors among us.
